notes.title: Key facts by topic
notes.html:
Motion & kinematics

  • Speed — Speed tells how far something goes in a certain time. Going 60 km in 2 hours is 30 kilometers every hour.
  • Velocity and direction — Velocity is speed with a direction. Walking 3 m/s north and 3 m/s south have the same speed but opposite velocities.
  • Acceleration — Acceleration is how fast velocity changes. A car going from 0 to 20 m/s in 4 s gains 5 m/s every second.

Forces & Newton’s laws

  • Pushes and pulls — A force is a push or a pull. It is measured in newtons (N). One newton is about the weight of a small apple.
  • Balanced and unbalanced forces — If forces balance, the motion does not change: a book on a table stays put. An unbalanced (net) force changes the motion.
  • Newton's first law — An object keeps doing what it is doing, at rest or moving in a straight line at steady speed, unless a net force acts on it. This is inertia.

Work, energy & power

  • Energy and work — Energy is the ability to make things change. Work is energy transferred by a force: lifting a box takes work.
  • Kinetic energy — Moving things have kinetic energy. It grows with mass and with the square of speed: doubling the speed makes the energy four times bigger.
  • Potential energy — Raised things can fall, so they store gravitational potential energy.

Momentum & collisions

  • Momentum — Momentum is mass times velocity. A heavy truck and a fast bullet can both be hard to stop.
  • Impulse — A force acting for a time changes momentum. A longer time means a smaller force for the same change, which is why airbags help.
  • Conservation of momentum — In a collision with no outside force, the total momentum before equals the total momentum after.

Circular motion & gravity

  • Going around — Anything moving in a circle is always turning, so its velocity keeps changing direction. That means it is accelerating even at constant speed.
  • Speed on a circle — One lap is 2πr long. If it takes time T, speed v = 2πr/T.
  • Centripetal acceleration — The acceleration points to the center and equals v²/r. The net force pointing in is the centripetal force, F = mv²/r.

Waves & sound

  • Waves carry energy — A wave moves energy without moving matter along with it. A stadium wave moves around the arena while each person only stands up and sits down.
  • Frequency and period — Frequency f is how many waves pass each second (hertz). Period T is the time for one wave. f = 1/T.
  • Wavelength and speed — The wavelength λ is the length of one wave. Wave speed = frequency × wavelength.

Light & optics

  • Light travels in straight lines — Light moves in straight rays at about 3 × 10⁸ m/s. We see an object when its light reaches our eyes. Shadows form where light is blocked.
  • Reflection — A ray hits a mirror and bounces off. The angle in equals the angle out, both measured from the normal (the line at 90° to the surface).
  • Refraction — Light bends when it passes between materials because it changes speed. The index of refraction is n = c/v. Snell's law links the angles.

Heat & thermodynamics

  • Heat and temperature — Temperature measures how fast the particles jiggle on average. Heat is energy that flows from hot to cold. Both are not the same thing.
  • Specific heat — Q = mcΔT gives the heat needed to change a temperature. Water has c = 4186 J/(kg·°C), which is why it warms slowly.
  • Phase changes — Melting or boiling takes energy with no temperature change. Q = mL, with L the latent heat. For water, L_fusion ≈ 334 kJ/kg and L_vaporization ≈ 2260 kJ/kg.

Electric fields & charge

  • Charge — Matter has positive and negative charge. Like charges repel, opposite charges attract. Charge is measured in coulombs (C). One electron has charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
  • Coulomb's law — The force between two point charges is F = kq₁q₂/r², with k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². Doubling the distance cuts the force to a quarter.
  • Electric field — The field E at a point is the force per unit charge, E = F/q. A point charge makes E = kQ/r². Field lines point away from positive charge.

Ohm’s law & DC circuits

  • Charge, current and voltage — Current is how much charge flows past a point each second. Voltage is the push that makes charge flow, like water pressure in a pipe.
  • Resistance — Resistance is how much a part holds back current, like a narrow pipe. It is measured in ohms (Ω).
  • Ohm's law — Voltage, current and resistance are linked: V = I × R. Double the voltage and the current doubles.

Kirchhoff & network analysis

  • Nodes and loops — A node is where wires meet. A loop is any closed path. Kirchhoff's two laws apply to every circuit, however tangled.
  • Current law — The current into a node equals the current out. Charge does not pile up.
  • Voltage law — Going once around any loop, the voltage rises equal the voltage drops. The sum is zero.

Capacitors, inductors & transients

  • Capacitor basics — A capacitor stores energy in an electric field. Q = CV and the energy is ½CV². Units: farads (F), often µF or nF.
  • RC charging — Through a resistor a capacitor charges gradually. The time constant is τ = RC. After one τ it reaches 63% of the final voltage; after 5τ it is essentially full.
  • RC discharging — Discharging, the voltage falls as V = V₀e^(−t/τ). After one τ it is 37% of the start.

AC, phasors & impedance

  • What AC means — Alternating current swings back and forth like a sine wave. Wall power is 60 Hz in the US: 60 full cycles each second.
  • RMS values — The RMS value gives the same heating as DC. For a sine wave V_rms = V_peak/√2 ≈ 0.707 V_peak. US outlets are 120 V rms.
  • Reactance — A capacitor resists AC by X_C = 1/(2πfC); an inductor by X_L = 2πfL. Units: ohms. Capacitors pass high frequencies, inductors pass low ones.

Resonance & filters

  • Frequency response — A filter treats frequencies differently. A low-pass filter keeps low frequencies, a high-pass keeps high ones, and a band-pass keeps a range.
  • RC cutoff — An RC filter drops to 70.7% (−3 dB) of the input at the cutoff frequency f_c = 1/(2πRC).
  • Decibels — Decibels compare sizes on a log scale: dB = 20 log₁₀(V_out/V_in) for voltage. Every factor of 10 is 20 dB; halving is about −6 dB.

Diodes, transistors & op-amps

  • Diodes — A diode lets current go one way. Silicon needs about 0.7 V forward; an LED needs roughly 2 V. Always add a series resistor.
  • LED resistor — The resistor drops the leftover voltage: R = (V_supply − V_LED)/I.
  • Rectifiers — A diode on an AC source blocks the negative half (half-wave). A bridge of four diodes flips the negative half (full-wave). A capacitor then smooths it.

Digital logic

  • Binary — Computers use only 0 and 1. Each place is a power of 2: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16... so 1011₂ = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11.
  • Hexadecimal — Hex uses 16 digits (0–9, A–F). One hex digit equals four bits: A = 1010, F = 1111.
  • Logic gates — AND is 1 only if both inputs are 1. OR is 1 if either is 1. NOT flips the bit. NAND and NOR are the opposites of AND and OR.

Magnetism & induction

  • Magnetic fields — Magnets and moving charges make magnetic fields, measured in tesla (T). Field lines run from north to south outside the magnet.
  • Force on a wire — A wire of length L carrying current I in a field B feels force F = BIL when the wire is at right angles to the field.
  • Force on a charge — A charge q moving at speed v across field B feels F = qvB. The force is sideways, so the charge goes in a circle of radius r = mv/(qB).

Power & transformers

  • Electric power — Power is P = VI = I²R = V²/R, in watts. A kilowatt-hour (kWh) is the energy of 1 kW used for 1 hour, or 3.6 million joules.
  • Why power lines use high voltage — Wire loss is I²R. Raising the voltage by 10× cuts the current for the same power by 10× and the loss by 100×.
  • Efficiency — Efficiency = useful output power ÷ input power. The difference leaves as heat.

written: Why do heavy and light objects fall together?
Gravity pulls harder on a heavier object, but a heavier object also resists acceleration more. The two effects cancel, so all objects fall with the same acceleration when air drag is ignored.
Why does a series circuit go dark when one bulb is removed?
There is only one path. Removing a part breaks the loop, so the current stops everywhere.

questions.q: A book rests on a table. What force pairs with the book's weight in Newton's third law: the table's push up on the book, or the book's pull on Earth?
text: gravitational pull of the book on earth
sol: Third-law pairs act on different objects.
Earth pulls the book down, so the book pulls Earth up. The table's push is a different interaction.
questions.w: Earth pulls the book down, so the book pulls Earth up. The table's push is a different interaction.

kin: Speed tells how far something goes in a certain time. Going 60 km in 2 hours is 30 kilometers every hour.
Velocity is speed with a direction. Walking 3 m/s north and 3 m/s south have the same speed but opposite velocities.
Acceleration is how fast velocity changes. A car going from 0 to 20 m/s in 4 s gains 5 m/s every second.
Near Earth, anything in free fall (no air drag) speeds up by about 9.8 m/s every second, no matter its mass.
When acceleration is steady: v = v₀ + at, and d = v₀t + ½at². Pick the one that has the quantities you know.
v = v₀ + at;  d = v₀t + ½at²
On a position-time graph, slope is velocity. On a velocity-time graph, slope is acceleration and area is displacement.
ohm: Current is how much charge flows past a point each second. Voltage is the push that makes charge flow, like water pressure in a pipe.
Resistance is how much a part holds back current, like a narrow pipe. It is measured in ohms (Ω).
Voltage, current and resistance are linked: V = I × R. Double the voltage and the current doubles.
In series there is one path. The same current goes through every part, resistances add, and voltages share the supply.
In parallel there are branches. Every branch gets the full supply voltage, and the currents add.
Power is how fast energy is used. A 60 W bulb uses 60 joules every second.
frc: A force is a push or a pull. It is measured in newtons (N). One newton is about the weight of a small apple.
If forces balance, the motion does not change: a book on a table stays put. An unbalanced (net) force changes the motion.
An object keeps doing what it is doing, at rest or moving in a straight line at steady speed, unless a net force acts on it. This is inertia.
The net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration. Push twice as hard and it accelerates twice as fast. Double the mass and it accelerates half as much.
Mass is how much matter you have (kg). Weight is the pull of gravity on it (N). Weight = mass × g, with g ≈ 10 N/kg near Earth.
Friction opposes sliding. Its maximum size is f = μN, where N is the push of the surface on the object and μ depends on the two surfaces.
When object A pushes on B, B pushes back on A with an equal and opposite force. The two forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel.
On a slope, gravity splits into a part along the slope, mg sin θ, and a part into the slope, mg cos θ.
nrg: Energy is the ability to make things change. Work is energy transferred by a force: lifting a box takes work.
Moving things have kinetic energy. It grows with mass and with the square of speed: doubling the speed makes the energy four times bigger.
Raised things can fall, so they store gravitational potential energy.
Energy is never created or destroyed. It changes form. Without friction, KE + PE stays the same along a path.
Power is how fast energy is used or work is done. One watt is one joule per second.
A stretched spring pulls back with F = kx and stores energy ½kx².
The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.
Efficiency = useful energy out ÷ energy in. No machine is 100% efficient because some energy always turns into heat.
mom: Momentum is mass times velocity. A heavy truck and a fast bullet can both be hard to stop.
A force acting for a time changes momentum. A longer time means a smaller force for the same change, which is why airbags help.
In a collision with no outside force, the total momentum before equals the total momentum after.
If objects stick, they move off together: m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = (m₁ + m₂)v. Kinetic energy is lost to heat and deformation.
In an elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are kept. Equal masses swap velocities.
If two objects start at rest and push apart, their momenta are equal and opposite. The lighter one moves faster.
A rocket pushes gas backward and gains forward momentum. It works in space because it does not push against anything outside.
On a force-time graph, the area under the curve is the impulse.
cir: Anything moving in a circle is always turning, so its velocity keeps changing direction. That means it is accelerating even at constant speed.
One lap is 2πr long. If it takes time T, speed v = 2πr/T.
The acceleration points to the center and equals v²/r. The net force pointing in is the centripetal force, F = mv²/r.
Centripetal force is not a new force. It is tension, gravity, friction or a normal force pointing toward the center.
Every pair of masses attracts. F = Gm₁m₂/r². Double the distance and the force becomes one quarter.
A satellite is falling around Earth. Gravity supplies the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r).
g = GM/r². Moving from the surface to twice the Earth's radius from the center makes g four times smaller.
At the top of a vertical loop, gravity and the normal force both point down. The slowest speed that keeps contact is v = √(gr).
wav: A wave moves energy without moving matter along with it. A stadium wave moves around the arena while each person only stands up and sits down.
Frequency f is how many waves pass each second (hertz). Period T is the time for one wave. f = 1/T.
The wavelength λ is the length of one wave. Wave speed = frequency × wavelength.
In a transverse wave the particles move sideways to the motion (light, a rope). In a longitudinal wave they move back and forth along it (sound).
Sound is a longitudinal wave in air. It travels about 340 m/s in air, faster in water and fastest in solids.
Waves add. Crest meets crest: bigger wave. Crest meets trough: they cancel. Two close frequencies make beats at |f₁ − f₂|.
On a string fixed at both ends, only certain waves fit: fₙ = n·v/(2L), n = 1, 2, 3, … This is how guitars and organs choose notes.
Intensity falls with the square of distance. Every 10 dB is ten times the intensity. A 10 dB increase sounds about twice as loud.
opt: Light moves in straight rays at about 3 × 10⁸ m/s. We see an object when its light reaches our eyes. Shadows form where light is blocked.
A ray hits a mirror and bounces off. The angle in equals the angle out, both measured from the normal (the line at 90° to the surface).
Light bends when it passes between materials because it changes speed. The index of refraction is n = c/v. Snell's law links the angles.
n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂
Going from a slow material to a faster one, the ray bends away from the normal. Past the critical angle sin θc = n₂/n₁ all the light reflects. Optical fibres use this.
A converging lens or concave mirror bends rays to a focus at distance f. The thin-lens equation connects object distance d₀, image distance dᵢ and focal length f.
thm: Temperature measures how fast the particles jiggle on average. Heat is energy that flows from hot to cold. Both are not the same thing.
Q = mcΔT gives the heat needed to change a temperature. Water has c = 4186 J/(kg·°C), which is why it warms slowly.
Melting or boiling takes energy with no temperature change. Q = mL, with L the latent heat. For water, L_fusion ≈ 334 kJ/kg and L_vaporization ≈ 2260 kJ/kg.
For a fixed amount of gas, PV/T stays constant, with T in kelvin. K = °C + 273. The ideal gas law is PV = nRT.
An engine takes heat Qh from a hot source, does work W and dumps Qc. Efficiency is e = W/Qh = 1 − Qc/Qh. The best possible efficiency is 1 − Tc/Th (kelvin).
